subject: religious-studies
title: Meta-Ethics: Cognitivism vs Non-Cognitivism
welcome_lead: Climb to the second floor of moral theory where meta-ethics asks not 'what should I do?' but 'what kind of thing is a moral judgement?'.
meta_desc: A-Level Edexcel Religious Studies adventure on meta-ethics: naturalism, intuitionism, emotivism, prescriptivism, and the open question argument.
final_note: You have surveyed the major meta-ethical positions on the status of moral language.

concepts.def: The view that moral statements express beliefs that can be true or false.
The view that moral statements express attitudes or commands rather than truth-apt beliefs.
The cognitivist view that moral properties are identical to natural properties.
Moore's charge that defining 'good' as any natural property commits a fallacy.
Moore's and Ross's view that we know basic moral truths by direct intellectual grasp.
Moore's test: for any natural property N, 'is N good?' remains an open question, so good is not identical to N.

walkthroughs.body_html: Ethical naturalists like Bentham identify good with the natural property of pleasure. G. E. Moore's Principia Ethica (1903) replies with the Open Question Argument: ask 'is pleasure good?' and the question remains genuinely open, which it would not if 'good' just meant 'pleasure'. Good, Moore concludes, is a simple, non-natural, indefinable property known by intuition.

H. A. Prichard argued that moral philosophy rests on a mistake when it tries to prove obligations; we apprehend duty directly. W. D. Ross, in The Right and the Good (1930), proposed seven prima facie duties (fidelity, reparation, gratitude, justice, beneficence, self-improvement, non-maleficence), known by reflection and weighed by judgement.

A. J. Ayer's emotivism (the 'boo-hurrah' theory) holds that 'stealing is wrong' expresses disapproval, not a proposition. Charles Stevenson refined this as a theory of moral persuasion. R. M. Hare's prescriptivism in The Language of Morals (1952) treats moral judgements as universalisable imperatives, retaining rational structure without truth-value.
